fields.Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "From a Golf Patent to the Zygote", "body": "Kallenbach traces his search to a golf company he launched at the 2008 PGA Show and a design patent he began to feel he did not really own. Years later, he says, he found the beginning of life itself: fertilization, where building materials from each parent become a zygote, a single cell holding all 46 chromosomes inside a membrane he likens to a fence around a biological estate. He drops the word conception, which he says has meant implantation since Roe v. Wade, and argues there is no calendar in the womb, joking that no squirrel wears a watch."}, {"title": "Why He Calls a Birthday a Cake", "body": "Kallenbach argues that the baby, the umbilical cord and the extra embryonic material are one unit, and that clamping and cutting the cord leaves the rest of the baby behind. In his reading the afterbirth, not the child, is what the birth certificate describes, and since he takes placenta to mean cake, every birthday celebrates the cake rather than the baby. That material dies within days, he says, becoming a decedent estate that needs fiduciaries, while the missing 40 weeks get filled by a straw man that disappears once the truth is known. His mantra: all present and accounted for from fertilization to last breath."}, {"title": "Reading Luke 5:31 as Wholeness", "body": "Reading from the King James Version, Kallenbach builds a long argument on Luke 5:31, \"They that are whole need not a physician.\" He argues that Jesus is both telling the whole they do not need him and claiming to be a physician, and he casts Jesus, the Lamb of God, as the amnion, the missing biology. The question being answered, in Luke 5:30, asks why Jesus eats with publicans and sinners; Kallenbach reads publicans as tax collectors, which he maps onto the Social Security number character, and sinners as debtors. Chance adds that much of the allegory concerns legal fiction versus natural law."}, {"title": "The Bar Association as a Hyphen", "body": "Kallenbach argues the cut creates two positions that do not exist in nature, the material left behind in the womb and the baby on the land, and that the Bar Association acts as the go-between, a ferryman across the River Styx reconnecting the man to his account. Picking up the image of the bar as a hyphen, he says the hyphen is the umbilical cord and a bond, and that like glue it is only needed when something is broken. Chance offers his own etymology, bar as son in Aramaic and kernel in Hebrew, tying it to Cronus, the scythe and the black robes."}, {"title": "Pursuing Truth Rather Than Freedom", "body": "Asked what a future parent should actually do about the cord and the afterbirth, Kallenbach says the easiest step is simply knowing your origin, and that in his view neither skipping the hospital nor leaving the cord on changes anything under the system as it stands. He asks whether any book in the Library of Congress can harm you and argues that no word on a document can hurt the living, who author their own lives. A tainted motive taints the outcome, he warns, and he frames the real choice as pursuing truth rather than freedom, since the truth is what makes you free."}]
fields.Intro Paragraph 1: Kurtis Kallenbach has spent years researching one deceptively simple question: what actually happened at the moment of your birth, biologically and legally, and what did you unknowingly give up?
fields.Intro Paragraph 2: His answer runs through embryology, maritime admiralty law, biblical allegory, and etymology. The zygote is your complete biological estate, every chromosome, encoded in one cell, bounded by the pelucid membrane like a property fence. The umbilical cord cut creates a legal severance between you and that origin. The birthday document registers the event in a maritime system that treats your body as cargo delivered to a berth. The amnion, the lamb of god, becomes a bounty. And knowing none of this is precisely how the system maintains its hold.

fields.Plus Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "Born Alive and the Placenta's Legal Title", "body": "Kallenbach walks through the legal term born alive, which defines a legal person as a product of conception, and then shows that conception in current law means implantation rather than fertilization. Because the placenta is the organ that evidences implantation, it is the thing born alive actually describes, so a title can be issued against it while the baby who came out whole is never covered at all. He pictures a glass marble pressed into a wall of clay, where the glass never mixes with the clay, to argue that the two biologies stay distinct."}, {"title": "The Author of Your Own Words", "body": "A long stretch of the second hour turns on authorship. Kallenbach insists that when he speaks as author the words mean what he says they mean and are not open to anyone else's interpretation, and that this authority only holds if he is the author from fertilization forward. Adopting the narrative handed over through the cut, he argues, makes you a character someone else wrote, which he likens to walking out the door dressed as Harry Potter and expecting J.K. Rowling not to demand a cut. Chance answers that the creator is God of whatever they create."}, {"title": "The Zygote Affidavit and the Letters", "body": "In October 2018 Kallenbach filed a forty page affidavit with his county records department evidencing his authority over the zygote, most of it legal definitions. He then describes a campaign of letters: three to the director of the Illinois Department of Public Health, who resigned, and one to the Secretary of Homeland Security, who he says resigned eleven days later, followed by letters to the National Security Council chairman and to the president. He claims the global economy shut down within a week of his third letter to Trump in March 2020, while stopping short of claiming he caused it."}, {"title": "Shipwreck, Salvage and the Phantom Limb", "body": "The maritime frame gets its fullest statement here. The capsule that implanted in the uterine wall is a boat that beaches and, left unclaimed, becomes a shipwreck available for admiralty salvage, while the baby outside the womb is treated as a pauper and a fugitive who needs salvation. Kallenbach then stacks three events from 1871: the District of Columbia Organic Act, the Haslam versus Lockwood ruling on abandoned waste material, and the coining of phantom limb. The cut cord, he argues, is both abandoned waste and a phantom limb that keeps haunting through the birth certificate."}, {"title": "The 1773 Memoir and the Republic of Letters", "body": "Closing on a question about the Salem witch trials and midwives, Kallenbach argues the midwives held control over whether the cord was cut at all. He then points to the 1773 Memoirs of the London Medical Society, which he says identified the cut material as an object of veneration, the Holy Grail in essence. Two of those men later signed the Declaration of Independence, and the republic that followed is in his reading a republic of letters, where the Bill of Rights protects only a living man whose constitution is mind, body and spirit rather than paper."}]
